title: Vision gone on waking, and the scalp hurts to comb
stem: A 74-year-old woman woke with painless loss of vision in the right eye. Six weeks of scalp tenderness on combing, jaw ache after chewing, weight loss and night sweats. BVA counting fingers OD, 20/25 OS. Right RAPD. Chalky pallid disc oedema OD with two flame haemorrhages, cup 0.2 OS. Macula and retinal vessels normal OD. ESR 78 mm/h, CRP 42 mg/L, platelets 486. Right temporal artery firm and non-pulsatile.

items.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.t: Non-arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy of the right optic nerve
Arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy, giant cell arteritis
Central retinal artery occlusion with secondary disc swelling
Demyelinating optic neuritis of the right optic nerve
Diabetic papillopathy with segmental oedema of the disc

items.short: Arteritic AION from giant cell arteritis
items.why: Chalky pallid oedema, vision at counting fingers and an RAPD point to arteritic infarction rather than a crowded-disc event. Jaw ache, scalp tenderness, ESR 78 and CRP 42 name the vasculitis.

dis.label: Non-arteritic AION
dis.tempting: Commoner, and it also gives sudden painless loss with disc oedema.
dis.ruled: Oedema here is chalky and pallid, with systemic symptoms and an ESR of 78.

dis.label: Retinal artery occlusion
dis.tempting: Sudden profound loss in an elderly arteritic patient fits an arterial event.
dis.ruled: No retinal opacification and no cherry-red spot; the lesion is a pallid swollen disc.

items.q: Which three findings separate an arteritic cause from a non-arteritic one?

options.t: Jaw ache after chewing for six weeks
Chalky pallid oedema of the swollen disc
ESR 78 mm/h with CRP 42 mg/L
Cup-to-disc ratio 0.2 in the fellow eye
Right relative afferent pupillary defect
Painless onset noticed on waking

items.short: Jaw claudication, pallid oedema, raised markers
items.why: Both entities give sudden painless loss with an RAPD and disc oedema. Jaw claudication, chalky pallor of the swelling and raised ESR and CRP are the arteritic markers.

dis.label: Small cup in fellow eye
dis.tempting: A crowded disc is a real risk marker, so it reads as supporting evidence.
dis.ruled: A small cup argues for the non-arteritic form, not against it.

dis.label: RAPD, painless onset
dis.tempting: Both are present and both are abnormal, so they read as diagnostic.
dis.ruled: Both occur in either form, so neither discriminates.

items.q: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.t: High-dose systemic corticosteroid today, biopsy within two weeks
Withhold systemic steroid until the temporal artery biopsy is reported
Oral prednisolone 20 mg daily with rheumatology review next week
Aspirin 300 mg daily and rheumatology review within 48 hours
Repeat ESR and CRP in 48 hours, then decide about steroid

items.short: Steroid now, biopsy within two weeks
items.why: Sight in the fellow eye is what is at risk and it can go within days. Steroid starts on clinical suspicion with an ESR of 78, and biopsy stays positive for one to two weeks after treatment begins.

dis.label: Wait for biopsy
dis.tempting: Confirming before committing an elderly patient to steroid feels careful.
dis.ruled: The fellow eye can infarct while waiting, and biopsy yield survives early steroid.

dis.label: Prednisolone 20 mg
dis.tempting: It treats, and a lower dose limits harm in a 74-year-old.
dis.ruled: Established visual loss needs high dose; 20 mg does not protect the other eye.

items.q: Which vascular event best explains the appearance of this disc?

options.t: Occlusion of the short posterior ciliary arteries
Thrombosis of the central retinal vein at the lamina
Embolic occlusion of a cilioretinal artery at the disc
Vasculitis of the pial vessels of the canalicular nerve
Stenosis of the internal carotid artery reducing perfusion

items.short: Short posterior ciliary artery occlusion
items.why: The laminar and prelaminar nerve is fed by the short posterior ciliary arteries. Granulomatous inflammation of these medium-sized vessels infarcts that watershed and gives pallid swelling.

dis.label: Central retinal vein
dis.tempting: Vein occlusion also swells the disc and drops vision suddenly.
dis.ruled: No dilated tortuous veins and no scattered retinal haemorrhages.

dis.label: Carotid stenosis
dis.tempting: Ocular ischaemic syndrome is real and she has vascular risk.
dis.ruled: It gives retinal signs and gradual change, not chalky disc pallor.

items.q: Ten days into high-dose steroid, which change most needs escalation?

options.t: Transient greying of the left eye with CRP risen to 38
Fasting glucose 9.2 mmol/L with nocturia since starting steroid
Insomnia, tremor and low mood since the steroid started
ESR fallen to 40 mm/h with the jaw ache still present
Right acuity unchanged at counting fingers since day one

items.short: Fellow eye symptoms with rising CRP
items.why: New obscurations in the uninvolved eye with a rising CRP mean active vasculitis and a second eye at risk. Steroid hyperglycaemia is managed alongside, not by cutting the dose.

dis.label: Glucose 9.2
dis.tempting: A real steroid effect that needs treatment and looks like a reason to taper.
dis.ruled: It calls for glycaemic control, not less steroid while sight is at risk.

dis.label: ESR 40, jaw ache
dis.tempting: A falling ESR reads as control, so the residual ache seems minor.
dis.ruled: Symptoms hold the taper where it is, but no visual threat means no escalation.

rules: If disc oedema is pallid, or comes with jaw claudication or scalp tenderness, start steroid before the biopsy. If the fellow eye reports obscurations, escalate the same day.

rows: Chalky pallid swelling, cup often spared
Hyperaemic segmental swelling in a small crowded disc
Counting fingers or worse in most eyes
Jaw ache, scalp tenderness, weight loss
ESR and CRP raised, platelets high
ESR and CRP normal for age
pair.decider: Raised ESR and CRP with jaw claudication move the case to same-day steroid and biopsy, whatever the disc looks like. Normal markers with a crowded fellow disc do not.

title: Headaches worst on waking, with a whoosh in both ears
stem: A 28-year-old woman has three months of daily headache, worst on waking and on coughing, with brief greyouts of vision on standing and a whooshing noise in both ears. Horizontal diplopia at distance. BMI 38. Doxycycline for four months. BVA 20/20 each, no RAPD. Bilateral disc oedema with obscured crossing vessels, no spontaneous venous pulsation. Abduction limited OS. Perimetry: enlarged blind spots, nasal step OS. BP 128/78.

items.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.t: Papilloedema from raised intracranial pressure
Bilateral optic neuritis of demyelinating origin
Buried optic disc drusen with pseudo-oedema
Malignant hypertension with bilateral disc swelling and exudates
Bilateral non-arteritic ischaemic optic neuropathy

items.short: Papilloedema, raised intracranial pressure
items.why: Positional headache, pulsatile tinnitus, obscurations and bilateral oedema with no venous pulsation are pressure signs. Preserved acuity with a sixth nerve deficit fits pressure, not neuritis.

dis.label: Bilateral optic neuritis
dis.tempting: A young woman with swollen discs and headache is the neuritis stereotype.
dis.ruled: Acuity is 20/20 with no RAPD and no pain on eye movement.

dis.label: Malignant hypertension
dis.tempting: It swells both discs and is the emergency nobody wants to miss.
dis.ruled: BP is 128/78, with no arteriolar narrowing and no exudates.

items.q: Which three steps belong in the initial workup?

options.t: MRI of the brain with venography to exclude venous thrombosis
Lumbar puncture with an opening pressure, after imaging
Stop the doxycycline and review the medication list
Start an oral corticosteroid taper for the disc oedema
Order carotid duplex ultrasound of both sides
Dispense base-out prism for the distance diplopia

items.short: MRI with venography, LP after imaging, stop the drug
items.why: Pressure has to be measured and secondary causes excluded before it is called idiopathic. Venous sinus thrombosis is the dangerous mimic, and tetracyclines are a recognised trigger.

dis.label: Steroid taper
dis.tempting: Steroid does lower pressure briefly and the discs look inflamed.
dis.ruled: It masks the picture, rebounds on withdrawal, and the weight gain worsens the disease.

dis.label: Prism for diplopia
dis.tempting: The diplopia is real and prism is the optometric reflex.
dis.ruled: The sixth nerve deficit resolves with the pressure, so prism chases a moving target.

items.q: Which mechanism explains the abduction deficit?

options.t: Stretch of the sixth nerve over the petrous ridge
Infarction of the sixth nerve nucleus in the dorsal pons
Restriction of the left medial rectus by an infiltrative myopathy
Compression of the nerve at the orbital apex by swollen muscle
Demyelinating plaque in the paramedian pontine reticular formation

items.short: Sixth nerve stretch from raised pressure
items.why: A raised pressure gradient displaces the brainstem downward and tethers the sixth nerve where it crosses the petrous ridge. That makes it a false localising sign rather than a second disease.

dis.label: Sixth nerve nucleus
dis.tempting: A nuclear lesion is the neat anatomical answer for an abduction deficit.
dis.ruled: Nuclear lesions give a gaze palsy, and there is no gaze or facial sign here.

dis.label: Medial rectus restriction
dis.tempting: Thyroid myopathy limits abduction and is common in young women.
dis.ruled: Nothing suggests restriction, and swollen discs with obscurations point intracranially.

items.q: Which change would move care to urgent surgical decompression?

options.t: Acuity falling to 20/60 with the field closing in ten days
Headache still present after two weeks of acetazolamide
Discs unchanged at six weeks with stable fields and acuity
Pulsatile tinnitus louder while acuity stays at 20/20
Weight unchanged after three months of dietary advice

items.short: Falling acuity with progressive field loss
items.why: Function decides. Loss of acuity and field over days is fulminant disease and needs shunting or optic nerve sheath fenestration, whereas headache and tinnitus alone do not.

dis.label: Headache at two weeks
dis.tempting: The symptom that brought her in has not improved, so treatment looks failed.
dis.ruled: Headache lags and has other causes, so it is not the surgical trigger.

dis.label: Discs unchanged
dis.tempting: Persistent oedema on examination reads as uncontrolled pressure.
dis.ruled: Oedema resolves slowly. Stable fields and acuity mean the nerve is coping.

items.q: Which finding would indicate buried disc drusen rather than true oedema?

options.t: Lumpy margin with autofluorescence and clear crossing vessels
Absent spontaneous venous pulsation on careful observation
Small crowded disc with no physiological cup and blurred margins
Peripapillary haemorrhage at the inferior disc margin
Transient greyouts of vision lasting a few seconds

items.short: Autofluorescent lumpy margin, vessels clear
items.why: Drusen elevate the disc without swelling the nerve fibre layer, so crossing vessels stay visible and the calcified bodies autofluoresce. Absent venous pulsation and a small cup occur in both.

dis.label: No venous pulsation
dis.tempting: Its absence is taught as the sign of raised pressure.
dis.ruled: It is absent in a fifth of normal eyes, so it cannot separate the two.

dis.label: Peripapillary bleed
dis.tempting: Haemorrhage looks like the active and dangerous option.
dis.ruled: Drusen bleed too, from the same crowded disc margin.

rules: If both discs are swollen with normal acuity, measure the pressure and image the venous sinuses before calling it idiopathic. If acuity or field falls over days, refer for decompression.

title: The lid that dropped with pain behind the eye
stem: A 58-year-old man has six hours of a drooping right lid, vertical and horizontal double vision, and severe pain behind the right eye. Smoker, hypertensive. Right ptosis 5 mm. The right eye rests down and out, with limited elevation, depression and adduction, and full abduction. Right pupil 6 mm, sluggish to light; left 3.5 mm, brisk. No RAPD. Deficit unchanged after 60 seconds of sustained upgaze. BP 168/96, glucose 6.1.

items.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.t: Pupil-involving third nerve palsy from an aneurysm
Microvascular ischaemic third nerve palsy sparing the pupil
Ocular myasthenia gravis with variable ptosis and diplopia
Cavernous sinus lesion involving the third and fourth nerves
Giant cell arteritis presenting as an ocular motor palsy

items.short: Aneurysmal pupil-involving third nerve palsy
items.why: A complete external palsy with a 6 mm sluggish pupil and abrupt severe pain is compression until imaging proves otherwise. A posterior communicating artery aneurysm is what must be excluded today.

dis.label: Microvascular palsy
dis.tempting: He is 58 and hypertensive, which is the vasculopathic profile exactly.
dis.ruled: The pupil is 6 mm and sluggish, and the glucose is 6.1.

dis.label: Ocular myasthenia
dis.tempting: Ptosis with diplopia and no visual loss is the myasthenic pattern.
dis.ruled: The pupil is involved and the deficit does not fatigue on upgaze.

items.q: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.t: Same-day CT angiography with neurosurgical referral
MRI of the brain booked within the next week
Observation for four weeks for spontaneous recovery
ESR, CRP and high-dose steroid started today
Fresnel prism now with review in two weeks

items.short: Same-day CT angiography, neurosurgery
items.why: A pupil-involving palsy with pain is a warning leak until proven otherwise, and the rupture risk is measured in hours. CT angiography is fast, available and sensitive for aneurysms of this size.

dis.label: MRI within a week
dis.tempting: MRI is the better parenchymal study and it does get imaging done.
dis.ruled: A week is longer than the interval in which these aneurysms rupture.

dis.label: Observe four weeks
dis.tempting: Microvascular palsies do recover in four to twelve weeks.
dis.ruled: Observation belongs to pupil-sparing palsies, and only after imaging.

items.q: Which three findings localise this to the nerve rather than muscle or junction?

options.t: Dilated pupil of 6 mm, sluggish to light
Down and out rest position with full abduction
Deficit constant through 60 seconds of upgaze
Ptosis of 5 mm on the affected side
Vertical and horizontal double vision
Severe pain behind the affected eye

items.short: Pupil involvement, down and out, no fatigue
items.why: Myasthenia never touches the pupil and it fatigues, while myopathy spares the pupil and ignores nerve territory. A fixed down and out eye with a sluggish pupil is a nerve trunk lesion.

dis.label: Ptosis 5 mm
dis.tempting: Ptosis is the headline sign and it is severe here.
dis.ruled: Levator weakness occurs in nerve, junction and muscle disease alike.

dis.label: Pain behind the eye
dis.tempting: Pain suggests compression, so it feels like a localiser.
dis.ruled: Pain tells you the cause is urgent, not where the lesion sits.

items.q: Why is the pupil involved in a compressive lesion of this nerve?

options.t: Pupillomotor fibres run superficially and are compressed first
The ciliary ganglion is carried inside the nerve sheath here
Parasympathetic axons are the most metabolically active fibres
Ischaemia of the vasa nervorum strikes the outer fibres first
Sympathetic fibres from the carotid plexus join the nerve trunk

items.short: Superficial pupillomotor fibres
items.why: The parasympathetic fibres travel on the dorsomedial surface of the nerve, fed by pial vessels. Extrinsic compression reaches them first, while microvascular disease infarcts the core.

dis.label: Vasa nervorum ischaemia
dis.tempting: It is the real mechanism of the vasculopathic palsy that spares the pupil.
dis.ruled: Ischaemia hits the central fibres, which is why the pupil is spared.

dis.label: Ciliary ganglion inside
dis.tempting: The ganglion does sit close to the inferior division route.
dis.ruled: It lies in the orbit behind the globe, not within the nerve trunk.

items.q: Angiography is negative. Which plan is most appropriate now?

options.t: Vascular risk review, occlusion or prism, reassess at six weeks
Repeat vascular imaging every week until recovery begins
Strabismus surgery once the deviation is measurable at six weeks
High-dose oral steroid for presumed inflammatory neuropathy
Botulinum toxin to the right lateral rectus this week

items.short: Risk review, prism or occlusion, six-week check
items.why: With imaging clear, a vasculopathic palsy is the working diagnosis and most recover by twelve weeks. Relief of diplopia is temporary while the angle changes, and the blood pressure is the treatable part.

dis.label: Surgery at six weeks
dis.tempting: The deviation is disabling and surgery is definitive.
dis.ruled: Wait at least six months for a stable measurement; most of this recovers.

dis.label: High-dose steroid
dis.tempting: Steroid is the reflex when a palsy fails to recover quickly.
dis.ruled: No inflammatory markers, no orbital signs, and it worsens his risk profile.

rules: If ptosis and an ocular motor deficit come with a dilated sluggish pupil, image the vessels the same day. If the pupil is spared in a vasculopath, imaging still comes before observation.

title: The smaller pupil that hides in the dark
stem: A 52-year-old smoker has three weeks of a drooping right upper lid, aching right-sided neck pain and a hoarse voice, with a cough for two months. BVA 20/20 each. Right upper lid sits 2 mm lower, right lower lid 1 mm higher. In dim light pupils are 2.5 mm OD and 4.0 mm OS; in bright light 3.0 mm and 4.2 mm. Right pupil takes over five seconds to dilate. Motility full, no proptosis, no RAPD.

items.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.t: Right oculosympathetic paresis, preganglionic
Physiological anisocoria with an involutional ptosis
Right tonic pupil with segmental iris palsy
Partial right third nerve palsy sparing motility
Pharmacological miosis from a topical agent

items.short: Right Horner syndrome, preganglionic
items.why: Ptosis with a raised lower lid, a smaller pupil in the dark and dilation lag are sympathetic denervation. Neck pain, hoarseness and cough put the lesion on the preganglionic run through the chest.

dis.label: Physiological anisocoria
dis.tempting: A fifth of people have it, and lid laxity at 52 is ordinary.
dis.ruled: Physiological anisocoria is equal in light and dark and has no dilation lag.

dis.label: Partial third palsy
dis.tempting: Ptosis plus anisocoria is the third nerve pattern.
dis.ruled: The wrong pupil is small here, and motility is full.

items.q: Which three findings place the lesion in the sympathetic pathway?

options.t: Anisocoria larger in dim light than in bright light
Right pupil takes over five seconds to dilate
Right lower lid sits 1 mm higher than the left
Right upper lid sits 2 mm lower than the left
Best corrected acuity of 20/20 in each eye
Full motility with no proptosis on either side

items.short: Dark anisocoria, dilation lag, raised lower lid
items.why: Sympathetic denervation weakens the dilator and Muller's muscle, so the deficit shows in the dark, dilation lags and the lower lid rises. Upper lid ptosis on its own has many causes.

dis.label: Upper lid 2 mm lower
dis.tempting: It is the sign that brought him in and it is on the affected side.
dis.ruled: Aponeurotic and mechanical ptosis do the same thing without pupil signs.

dis.label: 20/20, full motility
dis.tempting: Normal findings feel reassuring and therefore relevant.
dis.ruled: They exclude other disease but they localise nothing.

items.q: Which pharmacological test best confirms the diagnosis at this visit?

options.t: Apraclonidine 0.5% to both eyes, looking for reversal of anisocoria
Pilocarpine 0.125% to both eyes, looking for a supersensitive response
Phenylephrine 2.5% to both eyes, comparing the dilation achieved
Hydroxyamphetamine 1% to both eyes, comparing dilation of the two
Tropicamide 1% to both eyes, comparing the speed of dilation

items.short: Apraclonidine 0.5%, reversal confirms
items.why: Denervation supersensitivity of the dilator lets a weak alpha agonist reverse the anisocoria: the small pupil dilates and the ptosis lifts. Hydroxyamphetamine localises, but only after confirmation.

dis.label: Hydroxyamphetamine
dis.tempting: It is the classic Horner drop and it does separate the levels.
dis.ruled: It answers where, not whether, and it cannot be used on the same day.

dis.label: Pilocarpine 0.125%
dis.tempting: Dilute pilocarpine is a supersensitivity test, so the logic feels right.
dis.ruled: That test is for a tonic pupil, where the sphincter is denervated.

items.q: Which imaging plan is most appropriate?

options.t: CT of the neck and chest apex with carotid imaging, this week
MRI of the brain alone, arranged as an outpatient in one month
Carotid duplex ultrasound alone, arranged within one week
Chest radiograph now, with review in three months if normal
No imaging now, review in three months to see if the ptosis changes

items.short: Neck and chest apex imaging with carotid study
items.why: The sympathetic chain runs from hypothalamus to orbit, and a hoarse voice with neck pain in a smoker points at the apex and the carotid. Imaging has to cover the whole preganglionic route.

dis.label: Brain MRI alone
dis.tempting: Central lesions do cause Horner syndrome and MRI is the neuro study.
dis.ruled: The clues sit in the neck and chest, and a brain study misses both.

dis.label: No imaging
dis.tempting: Isolated Horner can be benign, and the signs are unchanged for weeks.
dis.ruled: Hoarseness, neck pain and a smoking history make observation unsafe.

items.q: Which change would make carotid dissection the leading concern?

options.t: Abrupt onset today with severe neck pain and pulsatile tinnitus
Gradual onset over three weeks with the voice unchanged throughout
Ipsilateral facial anhidrosis with a normal chest radiograph
Dilation lag of eight seconds instead of five in the dark
Weight loss of 4 kg with a cough productive of blood

items.short: Abrupt onset with neck pain and tinnitus
items.why: Dissection presents with sudden neck or facial pain, Horner syndrome within hours and pulsatile tinnitus, and it can embolise within days. Hoarseness and weight loss point instead to the apex.

dis.label: Weight loss, haemoptysis
dis.tempting: It is the most alarming option and it does signal serious disease.
dis.ruled: It points at an apical tumour, which is urgent but is not a dissection.

dis.label: Longer dilation lag
dis.tempting: A bigger number looks like a worse lesion.
dis.ruled: Lag grades the denervation, not the cause or the level.

rules: If anisocoria is greater in the dark and the pupil dilates late, call it sympathetic and confirm with apraclonidine. If the voice or the neck is involved, image the chest apex.

rows: Larger in dim light, with dilation lag
Equal in light and dark, no lag
Mild ptosis with the lower lid raised
Lid position normal or symmetrically lax
New, with neck, chest or vascular symptoms
pair.decider: Anisocoria that grows in the dark with dilation lag is denervation and needs imaging of the whole sympathetic chain. Anisocoria equal in light and dark needs nothing.

title: The lid that sits lower by the evening
stem: A 34-year-old woman has six weeks of a right lid that sits lower by the evening and intermittent vertical double vision that changes direction from day to day. No pain. BVA 20/20 each. Right ptosis 3 mm at rest, 4.5 mm after 45 seconds of sustained upgaze, with an upshoot of the lid on refixation. Ptosis 1 mm after a two-minute ice pack. Pupils equal and brisk. Orthophoric at one measurement, 6 Δ left hypertropia at the next.

items.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.t: Ocular myasthenia gravis, no bulbar signs
Aponeurotic ptosis with a decompensating phoria
Chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia
Partial right third nerve palsy, pupil sparing
Thyroid eye disease with an early restrictive myopathy

items.short: Ocular myasthenia gravis
items.why: Variable ptosis that worsens on sustained upgaze, a lid twitch on refixation, improvement after ice and a hypertropia that changes size are junctional fatigue. The pupils are always spared.

dis.label: Aponeurotic ptosis
dis.tempting: Ptosis worse by evening is what patients with lid laxity describe.
dis.ruled: Aponeurotic ptosis does not fatigue on upgaze or lift after an ice pack.

dis.label: External ophthalmoplegia
dis.tempting: It gives painless ptosis with motility loss and no pupil signs.
dis.ruled: It is slowly progressive and symmetrical, and it does not vary hourly.

items.q: Which three investigations are appropriate now?

options.t: Acetylcholine receptor antibody assay
CT of the chest to look for a thymoma
Repetitive nerve stimulation or single-fibre EMG
MRI of the orbits with fat suppression
ESR, CRP and temporal artery ultrasound
CT angiography of the circle of Willis

items.short: AChR antibodies, chest CT, nerve stimulation
items.why: Antibody testing confirms most cases, electrophysiology catches the seronegative ones, and a thymoma changes management in about one in ten. Orbital and vascular imaging answer a different question.

dis.label: Orbital MRI
dis.tempting: Ptosis with a variable vertical deviation looks orbital.
dis.ruled: Muscles and orbit are normal here; the fault is at the neuromuscular junction.

dis.label: CT angiography
dis.tempting: Ptosis with diplopia raises the aneurysm reflex.
dis.ruled: The pupils are equal and brisk and the signs fatigue with effort.

items.q: Which action matters most before she leaves today?

options.t: Safety-net for breathing and swallowing, with urgent routes
Dispense press-on prism for the vertical deviation now
Order a ptosis crutch to be fitted at the next visit
Arrange occlusion of the right eye until review in six months
Start a trial of pyridostigmine and review in four weeks

items.short: Safety-netting for bulbar and respiratory signs
items.why: About fifteen percent of ocular cases generalise within two years, and a crisis is a respiratory emergency. She needs to know which symptoms mean the emergency department rather than the clinic.

dis.label: Press-on prism now
dis.tempting: The diplopia is the complaint and prism is the optical fix.
dis.ruled: A deviation that changes within the day cannot be prismed reliably.

dis.label: Start pyridostigmine
dis.tempting: It is the right drug class for the disease.
dis.ruled: Prescribing sits with the neurologist, and it is not today's priority.

items.q: Which mechanism explains the fatigue on sustained upgaze?

options.t: Antibodies block postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors
Antibodies attack presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels
Deletion of mitochondrial DNA in extraocular muscle fibres
Segmental demyelination of the superior division of the third nerve
Depletion of acetylcholinesterase in the synaptic cleft

items.short: Postsynaptic receptor blockade
items.why: Receptor loss lowers the endplate potential, so repeated release fails to reach threshold as vesicle stores run down. Rest and cooling restore transmission, which is why ice lifts the lid.

dis.label: Calcium channel antibody
dis.tempting: It is a real antibody-mediated junction disease with weakness.
dis.ruled: That is Lambert-Eaton: strength improves with use and reflexes are lost.

dis.label: Mitochondrial deletion
dis.tempting: It is the mechanism of the disease this most resembles on inspection.
dis.ruled: Mitochondrial ptosis is fixed and progressive, never fatiguable.

items.q: Which single finding would argue hardest against this diagnosis?

options.t: A fixed right pupil of 6 mm with a poor light reaction
Weakness of orbicularis oculi on forced lid closure
A hypertropia that measures differently on two days
Improvement of the ptosis after a two-minute ice pack
Normal deep tendon reflexes throughout the four limbs

items.short: A fixed, poorly reactive pupil
items.why: The iris sphincter is not affected in myasthenia, so pupil involvement forces a different diagnosis. Orbicularis weakness and day-to-day variability are typical rather than exclusionary.

dis.label: Orbicularis weakness
dis.tempting: Extra weakness sounds like a bigger and different disease.
dis.ruled: Orbicularis involvement is common in ocular myasthenia and supports it.

dis.label: Normal reflexes
dis.tempting: Normal reflexes seem to rule out a neuromuscular disorder.
dis.ruled: Reflexes are normal in myasthenia and lost in Lambert-Eaton.

rules: If ptosis varies within the hour, fatigues on upgaze or lifts after ice, test for myasthenia and image the chest. If the pupil is involved, it is not myasthenia.

title: The print that slides together after twenty minutes
stem: A 19-year-old student has four months of print that blurs and slides together after twenty minutes of reading, with frontal headache that eases when one eye is covered. BVA 20/20 each, refraction +0.25 DS each. Cover test orthophoric at distance, 12 Δ exophoria at near. Near point of convergence 14 cm break, 18 cm recovery. Positive fusional vergence at near: blur 8, break 12, recovery 4. Amplitude of accommodation 11 D each.

items.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.t: Convergence insufficiency with a remote near point
Accommodative insufficiency with reduced amplitude
Basic exophoria equal at distance and at near
Divergence excess intermittent exotropia
Convergence paresis from a dorsal midbrain lesion

items.short: Convergence insufficiency
items.why: An exophoria that appears only at near, a near point of 14 cm and positive vergence breaking at 12 are the findings that define it. Accommodation measures 11 D, which is normal at 19.

dis.label: Accommodative insufficiency
dis.tempting: Blur at near after twenty minutes is the classic accommodative complaint.
dis.ruled: Amplitude is 11 D, which is age-normal, and the exophoria is at near only.

dis.label: Basic exophoria
dis.tempting: There is an exophoria, and the near symptoms fit an exodeviation.
dis.ruled: The distance cover test is orthophoric, so the deviation is not equal.

items.q: Which three findings support this rather than an accommodative cause?

options.t: Near point of convergence 14 cm with recovery at 18 cm
Exophoria of 12 Δ at near with orthophoria at distance
Positive fusional vergence at near breaking at 12 Δ
Amplitude of accommodation of 11 D in each eye
Refraction of +0.25 DS with 20/20 in each eye
Frontal headache after twenty minutes of reading

items.short: Remote near point, near exophoria, low vergence
items.why: Both conditions blur print, so the separation sits in the vergence data: a remote near point, an exodeviation confined to near, and a reduced positive fusional range. Amplitude is age-normal.

dis.label: Amplitude 11 D
dis.tempting: It is the accommodative measurement, so it looks decisive here.
dis.ruled: By Hofstetter the minimum at 19 is about 10 D, so 11 D is normal.

dis.label: Refraction, headache
dis.tempting: Both are in the record and both feel relevant to near work.
dis.ruled: Neither separates the two, because both occur with either mechanism.

items.q: Which management has the best evidence as first-line here?

options.t: Office-based vergence therapy with home reinforcement
Base-in prism at near, prescribed by Sheard's criterion
Plus addition at near of +1.00 D for reading tasks
Home pencil push-ups alone, five minutes twice daily
Referral for bilateral medial rectus resection surgery

items.short: Office-based vergence therapy
items.why: Supervised in-office therapy with home reinforcement outperformed pencil push-ups and placebo in the CITT trial. Prism and plus adds treat the symptom without restoring fusional range.

dis.label: Push-ups alone
dis.tempting: They are free, familiar and easy to instruct in a single visit.
dis.ruled: In the trial push-ups alone performed no better than placebo therapy.

dis.label: Base-in prism
dis.tempting: It relieves symptoms immediately and is easy to dispense.
dis.ruled: It leaves the vergence deficit untreated, so the demand returns.

items.q: Twelve weeks of therapy done well and symptoms persist. What next?

options.t: Reassess, then add base-in prism if the near point stays remote
Repeat the same twelve-week therapy programme without changes
Refer for surgery on the horizontal muscles at near
Prescribe a +1.50 near addition and stop the therapy
Discharge with reassurance that the condition is benign

items.short: Reassess, then prism if measures unchanged
items.why: Therapy is judged on the measures, not the calendar. If the near point and the fusional range have not moved, prism supports the deficit, whereas repeating a failed programme costs months.

dis.label: Repeat unchanged
dis.tempting: Persistence is often the answer with therapy that works slowly.
dis.ruled: Twelve weeks done well with no change in the measures is a failed course.

dis.label: Discharge
dis.tempting: The condition is benign and no pathology has been found.
dis.ruled: The symptoms are disabling for a student and they persist untreated.

items.q: Her college asks for a report on her reading difficulty. What is required?

options.t: Written authorisation from the patient before releasing a report
Verbal consent recorded in the notes at the time of the request
Nothing, since the request comes from her educational institution
Written authorisation from a parent, as she is still a student
A summary with the identifiers removed, sent without consent

items.short: Written patient authorisation first
items.why: She is an adult, so the record is hers to release. Authorisation is written, specific to the recipient, and filed with the record; the request itself creates no permission.

dis.label: College request alone
dis.tempting: Educational requests feel administrative rather than clinical.
dis.ruled: A third party gains no right of access by asking on its own letterhead.

dis.label: Parental authorisation
dis.tempting: Student status suggests a parent is still the responsible party.
dis.ruled: At 19 she consents for herself, whoever pays the fees.

rules: If exophoria appears only at near with a remote near point, treat the vergence system before reaching for prism. If twelve weeks of therapy moves no measure, then add prism.

title: The eye that turns in over a picture book
stem: A 4-year-old boy has six months of an inward turn of the right eye, noticed over picture books and worse when he is tired. Cycloplegic retinoscopy +5.00 DS OD, +4.75 DS OS. Uncorrected cover test 20 Δ esotropia at distance, 30 Δ at near. With the full plus in trial frames, 4 Δ esophoria at distance and 8 Δ esotropia at near. Crowded acuity 20/30 OD, 20/25 OS. Stereopsis 400 seconds of arc. Fundi normal.

items.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.t: Refractive accommodative esotropia, convergence excess
Non-accommodative convergence excess with a high AC/A ratio
Infantile esotropia that has presented late to care
Partial right sixth nerve palsy with an incomitant deviation
Sensory esotropia from untreated unilateral amblyopia

items.short: Refractive accommodative esotropia
items.why: Uncorrected hypermetropia of +5.00 D with 20 Δ at distance collapsing to 4 Δ esophoria under the full plus makes the deviation accommodative. The residual 8 Δ at near marks the excess.

dis.label: Non-accommodative excess
dis.tempting: There is a genuine near excess of 8 Δ after correction.
dis.ruled: That entity carries little hypermetropia and does not respond to plus.

dis.label: Infantile esotropia
dis.tempting: A large esotropia in a small child fits the label loosely.
dis.ruled: Onset near three and a half years, and the response to plus, exclude it.

items.q: What is the most appropriate first management?

options.t: Full cycloplegic plus worn constantly, review in six weeks
Half the cycloplegic plus, to preserve some fusional drive
Full correction with a +2.50 bifocal add from the start
Part-time occlusion of the left eye for two hours daily
Referral for bilateral medial rectus recession surgery

items.short: Full cycloplegic plus, constant wear
items.why: The deviation is driven by accommodative effort, so removing the effort with the full plus is the treatment. Six weeks lets alignment and acuity respond before anything is added.

dis.label: Half the plus
dis.tempting: Undercorrecting a hypermetrope is a familiar habit from adult practice.
dis.ruled: Any residual accommodative demand keeps driving the esotropia.

dis.label: Bifocal from the start
dis.tempting: There is a near excess, and a bifocal treats it directly.
dis.ruled: Measure the residual near angle on full plus first, because it often settles.

items.q: Which three findings show the deviation is accommodative in origin?

options.t: Cycloplegic refraction of +5.00 DS in the right eye
Distance deviation falls to 4 Δ with the full plus
Esotropia larger at near than at distance untreated
Crowded acuity of 20/30 in the right eye
Stereopsis of 400 seconds of arc on testing
Onset noticed six months ago, worse when tired

items.short: High hypermetropia, plus response, near excess
items.why: The response to plus proves the mechanism, supported by significant hypermetropia and a deviation larger at near. Acuity and stereopsis measure the cost of the deviation, not its cause.

dis.label: Acuity 20/30
dis.tempting: Reduced acuity in the deviating eye looks like the key abnormality.
dis.ruled: It measures amblyopia risk, not what drives the deviation.

dis.label: Onset six months ago
dis.tempting: Age of onset is how esotropias are usually classified.
dis.ruled: Onset narrows the list but proves nothing about accommodation.

items.q: Which mechanism links the refractive error to the deviation?

options.t: Accommodative effort drives convergence by the AC/A link
Reduced negative fusional vergence range at near fixation
Immature divergence tone in the developing vergence system
Bilateral lateral rectus underaction from a mild deficit
Sensory deprivation from the anisometropia between the two eyes

items.short: Accommodative convergence through AC/A
items.why: Each dioptre of accommodation carries a fixed quantity of convergence. To clear +5.00 D of hypermetropia the child accommodates hard, and the linked convergence overwhelms fusional divergence.

dis.label: Low negative vergence
dis.tempting: Negative fusional vergence is what would hold an esodeviation latent.
dis.ruled: That is the reserve that fails, not the drive that creates the deviation.

dis.label: Sensory deprivation
dis.tempting: There is 0.25 D of anisometropia and unequal acuity.
dis.ruled: Deprivation esotropia needs poor vision in one eye, not 20/30.

items.q: Six weeks on full plus: aligned at distance, 12 Δ esotropia at near. What next?

options.t: Add a +2.50 flat-top bifocal with the segment splitting the pupil
Increase the distance plus by 1.00 D over the cycloplegic finding
Prescribe 8 Δ base-out prism divided between the two eyes
Start part-time occlusion of the left eye for the near deviation
Refer for surgery on the medial recti for the residual angle

items.short: +2.50 bifocal, segment splitting the pupil
items.why: A residual near esotropia on full distance correction is a high AC/A, treated by removing the near accommodative demand. The segment has to sit high enough to be used, at the pupil margin.

dis.label: Extra 1.00 D of plus
dis.tempting: More plus relaxes more accommodation, so it looks like the same logic.
dis.ruled: It blurs distance vision without touching the near excess.

dis.label: Surgery now
dis.tempting: Twelve prism dioptres at near is a real deviation.
dis.ruled: Optical treatment is incomplete, and a bifocal usually aligns the near angle.

rules: If an esotropia shrinks under the full cycloplegic plus, accommodative drive is the disease. If the near angle persists on full plus, add a bifocal rather than more distance plus.

title: The head tilt that started after the bicycle fall
stem: A 22-year-old man has three weeks of vertical double vision since a fall from his bicycle with brief loss of consciousness. Worst looking down, and he misjudges stairs. Head tilted to the left. Right hypertropia 8 Δ in primary position, 14 Δ in left gaze, 18 Δ on right head tilt, 4 Δ on left tilt. Depression in adduction limited OD. Excyclotorsion 8 ° on double Maddox rod. Vertical fusion range 4 Δ.

items.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.t: Acquired right fourth nerve palsy after head trauma
Decompensated congenital right fourth nerve palsy
Right skew deviation from a posterior fossa lesion
Right Brown syndrome limiting elevation in adduction
Thyroid eye disease restricting the right inferior rectus

items.short: Traumatic right fourth nerve palsy
items.why: The three-step pattern is a right hypertropia worse in left gaze and on right tilt, with limited depression in adduction. Symptomatic extorsion and a 4 Δ fusion range date it to the injury.

dis.label: Congenital fourth palsy
dis.tempting: Trauma often decompensates a long-standing palsy, and the pattern matches.
dis.ruled: A congenital palsy carries a large vertical fusion range and no torsional symptoms.

dis.label: Skew deviation
dis.tempting: Head trauma with a vertical deviation does raise a central cause.
dis.ruled: Skew gives intorsion of the higher eye and no dependence on head tilt.

items.q: Which three findings favour an acquired palsy over a decompensated congenital one?

options.t: Symptomatic excyclotorsion of 8 ° on double Maddox rod
Vertical fusion range of only 4 Δ
Onset dated to a head injury three weeks ago
Right hypertropia increasing on right head tilt
Habitual head tilt towards the left shoulder
Right hypertropia increasing in left gaze

items.short: Torsion, small fusion range, dated onset
items.why: The three-step results and the head tilt are shared by both forms, so they cannot separate them. Torsional symptoms, a small vertical fusion range and a dated onset belong to the acquired palsy.

dis.label: Three-step results
dis.tempting: They are how the palsy is identified, so they look like the answer.
dis.ruled: Both forms give the same pattern, which names the muscle and nothing else.

dis.label: Habitual head tilt
dis.tempting: A tilt suggests a posture adopted over many years.
dis.ruled: New palsies adopt a tilt within days, so a tilt dates nothing.

items.q: What is the most appropriate management now?

options.t: Occlusion or Fresnel prism, reassess at three months
Ground-in vertical prism in new spectacles today
Surgery on the right inferior oblique within a month
Botulinum toxin to the right inferior oblique now
Neurosurgical referral for the head injury this week

items.short: Temporary prism or occlusion, review at 3 months
items.why: Traumatic fourth nerve palsies improve for up to six months, so the measurement to operate on does not exist yet. Temporary relief keeps him functional while the angle changes.

dis.label: Ground-in prism now
dis.tempting: It gives comfortable single vision and looks like definitive care.
dis.ruled: The deviation is still changing, so the prescription will soon be wrong.

dis.label: Early surgery
dis.tempting: Three weeks of disabling diplopia feels like enough waiting.
dis.ruled: Spontaneous recovery is common, so operate only on a stable measurement.

items.q: What does the head tilt test measure in this patient?

options.t: Right intorters compete on right tilt, so the superior rectus elevates
Right extorters compete on right tilt, so the inferior oblique elevates
The vertical fusional range available in each head position
Vestibulo-ocular gain during a slow head roll manoeuvre
The comitance of the deviation between the two lateral gazes

items.short: Intorters compete, superior rectus unopposed
items.why: Tilting to the right calls on the right intorters, superior oblique and superior rectus. With the oblique palsied the superior rectus elevates unopposed, so the hypertropia grows.

dis.label: Extorters on right tilt
dis.tempting: Naming the other torsional pair sounds equally plausible.
dis.ruled: Extorters act on tilt to the other side, which is why the deviation falls there.

dis.label: Vertical fusion range
dis.tempting: Fusion range is measured in this workup and it matters here.
dis.ruled: Range is measured with prism, not by tilting the head.

items.q: Which finding would point to skew deviation instead?

options.t: Incyclotorsion of the higher eye with a contralateral head tilt
Excyclotorsion of the higher eye measured on Maddox rod
Hypertropia that increases on head tilt towards the higher eye
Limited depression of the higher eye in adduction
Vertical deviation that is larger in contralateral gaze

items.short: Incyclotorsion of the higher eye
items.why: Skew is a central prenuclear imbalance and produces an ocular tilt reaction: the higher eye intorts and the head tilts towards the lower eye. A palsied superior oblique lets the eye extort.

dis.label: Excyclotorsion
dis.tempting: Torsion is the discriminator, so any torsion looks like the answer.
dis.ruled: Direction decides: extorsion of the higher eye is the fourth nerve palsy.

dis.label: Limited depression
dis.tempting: It is an underaction, and underactions occur in central disease too.
dis.ruled: Depression failing in adduction is superior oblique weakness itself.

rules: If a vertical deviation follows the three-step pattern with symptomatic extorsion, it is an acquired fourth nerve palsy. If the torsion runs the other way, think skew and image.

rows: Higher eye intorted, part of a tilt reaction
Away from the palsy, relieves the torsion
Towards the lower eye, with a body lean
pair.decider: The direction of torsion separates them: extorsion of the higher eye is a superior oblique palsy, intorsion is a skew and needs posterior fossa imaging.

title: The prescription that has moved twice this year
stem: A 9-year-old girl reports distance blur. Her spectacles from a year ago read -1.25 DS each; cycloplegic refraction today is -2.50 DS OD and -2.75 DS OS. Axial length 24.30 mm OD and 24.40 mm OS, up 0.45 mm in the year. Both parents are myopic. She spends under an hour outdoors and about four hours on near work daily. Corrected acuity 20/20 each, orthophoric, accommodative lag +0.75 D. Fundi normal.

items.q: Which feature best predicts continued progression here?

options.t: Axial elongation of 0.45 mm in the year at age nine
Two myopic parents in the immediate family history
Spherical equivalent of -2.50 D at the present visit
Four hours of daily near work with little time outdoors
Accommodative lag of +0.75 D at the near point

items.short: 0.45 mm of axial elongation in a year
items.why: Progression is measured as axial growth, and 0.45 mm in a year at nine is roughly twice the expected rate. History and habits raise risk but they do not measure what this eye is doing.

dis.label: Two myopic parents
dis.tempting: Parental myopia is the best-known risk factor for onset.
dis.ruled: It predicts who becomes myopic, not how fast this eye is growing.

dis.label: Accommodative lag
dis.tempting: Lag theories of progression are still widely taught.
dis.ruled: Lag has not predicted progression in trials, and 0.75 D is unremarkable.

items.q: Which single change has been shown to slow axial elongation?

options.t: Low-dose atropine 0.05% at night to both eyes
Undercorrection of the distance prescription by 0.75 D
Single vision spectacles worn at the full correction
A progressive addition lens for the accommodative lag
Vergence therapy to reduce the accommodative demand

items.short: Low-dose atropine 0.05% nightly
items.why: Only low-dose atropine here has slowed axial growth; orthokeratology and dual-focus soft lenses are the other proven options. Undercorrection accelerates progression and single vision is the comparator.

dis.label: Undercorrection
dis.tempting: Less minus feels like less stimulus for the eye to grow.
dis.ruled: Trials showed faster progression with undercorrection, not slower.

dis.label: Progressive addition lens
dis.tempting: Reducing the near demand is a plausible mechanism and is well marketed.
dis.ruled: The effect measured in trials is small and does not change management.

items.q: What is the most appropriate plan at this visit?

options.t: Full correction, a control option chosen, axial length at six months
Full correction now, with review of the refraction in twelve months
Atropine 1% at night with photochromic lenses for the glare
Undercorrect by 0.50 D and increase time outdoors to two hours daily
Orthokeratology fitted today without discussing the alternatives

items.short: Correct fully, start control, remeasure at six months
items.why: She is progressing fast enough to treat, so the visit ends with a chosen intervention, advice on outdoor time, and a measurement interval short enough to judge the effect.

dis.label: Review in a year
dis.tempting: Annual review is the routine interval for a child in spectacles.
dis.ruled: Another 0.45 mm of growth passes before anyone notices the failure.

dis.label: Atropine 1%
dis.tempting: The strongest concentration should give the largest effect.
dis.ruled: It brings glare, near blur and marked rebound for little extra benefit.

items.q: At six months on atropine 0.05%, axial length is up 0.25 mm. What next?

options.t: Check compliance, then consider adding an optical treatment
Stop treatment, since this elongation shows the drop has failed
Increase the atropine concentration to 1% each night
Continue unchanged and remeasure in a further twelve months
Switch to single vision spectacles and advise outdoor time

items.short: Confirm compliance, then combine treatments
items.why: A quarter of a millimetre in six months is inadequate control, and the two commonest reasons are missed doses and too weak a stimulus. Combination therapy is the next step, not a stronger drop.

dis.label: Atropine 1%
dis.tempting: Escalating the dose is the reflex when a drug underperforms.
dis.ruled: Side effects rise steeply and rebound is worse, so combine instead.

dis.label: Remeasure in a year
dis.tempting: Trends need time, and a single measurement can mislead.
dis.ruled: The trend is already unfavourable, and twelve months loses the window.

items.q: Which three duties apply when starting the atropine off-label?

options.t: Explain that the use is outside the licensed indication
Record the parent's informed consent in the clinical notes
Document the alternatives offered and the review interval
Notify the state board of optometry of the prescription
Obtain a second practitioner's signature before prescribing
Ask the child to countersign the consent entry herself

items.short: Disclose off-label use, consent, document alternatives
items.why: Off-label prescribing is lawful where it is clinically justified. The duty is disclosure of licensing status and alternatives, consent from the person with parental responsibility, and a record of both.

dis.label: Notify the board
dis.tempting: Regulatory notification sounds like the safe and compliant step.
dis.ruled: No such duty exists for prescribing within scope of practice.

dis.label: Child countersigns
dis.tempting: Involving the child respects her developing autonomy.
dis.ruled: At nine she assents, while consent is the parent's to give and record.

rules: If axial length rises more than 0.20 mm in six months, treat rather than watch. If the drop is used off-label, record the licensing status, the alternatives and the consent.

title: The new spectacles that double the print
stem: A 58-year-old woman cannot tolerate new single vision spectacles: R +5.00 DS, L +1.00 DS, optical centres set at her distance interpupillary distance. She reads with her eyes 8 mm below the optical centres. Print doubles vertically after a minute of reading. Corrected acuity 20/20 each. Cover test orthophoric at distance, 2 Δ exophoria at near. Vertical fusion range 2 Δ. Frame well adjusted, vertex distance equal.

items.q: By Prentice's rule, what vertical imbalance does the reading position induce?

options.t: 0.8 Δ, base up before the right eye
1.6 Δ, base up before the right eye
3.2 Δ, base up before the right eye
4.0 Δ, base up before the right eye
4.8 Δ, base up before the right eye

items.short: 3.2 Δ net, base up before the right eye
items.why: Prism equals decentration in centimetres times lens power. Right 0.8 cm x 5.00 D gives 4.0 Δ base up, left 0.8 cm x 1.00 D gives 0.8 Δ base up, so the net imbalance is 3.2 Δ.

dis.label: 4.0 Δ
dis.tempting: It is the prism induced by the right lens, correctly calculated.
dis.ruled: The left lens induces 0.8 Δ the same way, and only the difference counts.

dis.label: 4.8 Δ
dis.tempting: Adding the two prisms feels right when both eyes are affected.
dis.ruled: Both bases are up, so the two prisms subtract rather than add.

items.q: What explains the diplopia at the reading position?

options.t: Induced vertical imbalance exceeding her vertical fusion range
A decompensating vertical phoria unmasked by new spectacles
A mild right superior oblique palsy revealed by near work
Incorrect interpupillary distance creating a horizontal imbalance
Aniseikonia from the difference in spectacle magnification

items.short: Induced imbalance beats the fusion range
items.why: Vertical fusional amplitude is small, 2 Δ here, and the reading position generates 3.2 Δ. The deviation appears only in downgaze, which is why her distance vision is comfortable.

dis.label: Decompensating phoria
dis.tempting: New spectacles often unmask a phoria, and the timing fits exactly.
dis.ruled: The distance cover test is orthophoric and the symptom is position dependent.

dis.label: Superior oblique palsy
dis.tempting: Vertical diplopia worst on reading is the palsy's textbook symptom.
dis.ruled: No torsion, no gaze or tilt pattern, and it began with the new lenses.

items.q: Which three changes would reduce the imbalance at the reading position?

options.t: A separate near pair with centres set at the reading position
Slab-off on the more plus lens if a bifocal is dispensed
Contact lens correction of the anisometropia for near work
A larger frame with a higher fitting cross position
Reducing the vertex distance by 2 mm at both eyes
Polycarbonate lenses to reduce the lens thickness

items.short: Near pair, slab-off, contact lenses
items.why: The imbalance is decentration multiplied by unequal power, so each fix removes one of the two: centre the lenses where she looks, cancel the difference, or move the correction to the cornea.

dis.label: Higher fitting cross
dis.tempting: Adjusting the fitting height does sound like the lever to pull.
dis.ruled: Raising the centres increases the drop in downgaze and the imbalance with it.

dis.label: Polycarbonate lenses
dis.tempting: Thinner lighter lenses do improve tolerance of an anisometropic Rx.
dis.ruled: Material changes cosmetics and weight, never the induced prism.

items.q: Which single solution is most appropriate for her reading?

options.t: A dedicated near pair centred at the reading position
Grind 3 Δ base down into the right distance lens
Reduce the right lens to +4.00 DS to balance the prisms
Add 3 Δ base in at near, split between the lenses
A smaller frame with a higher fitting cross for both eyes

items.short: Dedicated near pair, centres lowered
items.why: Centring each lens where she looks removes the decentration, and with it the induced prism, without touching her distance correction or her acuity in either eye.

dis.label: Reduce the right power
dis.tempting: Equalising the powers does remove the imbalance arithmetically.
dis.ruled: It leaves the right eye 1.00 D under-corrected and blurred at all distances.

dis.label: Base-down in the right
dis.tempting: Prescribing the opposing prism looks like a direct correction.
dis.ruled: It corrects downgaze and breaks fusion at distance, where she is comfortable.

items.q: Which dispensing check would have caught this before collection?

options.t: Compute the induced prism at the near gaze position
Verify the back vertex distance at both eyes
Confirm the interpupillary distance to 1 mm
Check the base curve matches the previous pair
Measure the pantoscopic tilt and adjust the pads

items.short: Calculate induced prism at the near position
items.why: With 4.00 D of anisometropia, any vertical drop below the optical centres creates imbalance, so the calculation belongs at the design stage, before the lenses are cut and glazed.

dis.label: Vertex distance
dis.tempting: Vertex distance matters at these powers and is easy to check.
dis.ruled: It changes effective power, not the prism induced by decentration.

dis.label: IPD to 1 mm
dis.tempting: Centration error is the problem, so a PD check feels right.
dis.ruled: Horizontal centration is correct here, and the drop is vertical.

rules: If lens powers differ by more than 1.00 D, compute the induced prism at the reading position before dispensing. If it exceeds the vertical fusion range, centre a separate near pair.
